register: wave-5 authoring register (S-B5 tranche) — part 2 of 2

items.stem: Define thermal decomposition.
items.modelAnswer: Thermal decomposition is the breaking down of a substance due to the action of heat.

items.stem: State the general pattern for heating a metal carbonate that decomposes.
items.modelAnswer: A metal carbonate breaks down to give a metal oxide and carbon dioxide.

items.stem: Explain why copper(II) carbonate decomposes on heating while sodium carbonate, from the top of the reactivity series, resists the flame.
items.modelAnswer: Carbonates of the less reactive metals, those low in the series, break apart on heating; copper sits low in the reactivity series so its carbonate decomposes, while sodium sits at the very top, so its carbonate holds together.

items.stem: A heated tube holds a decomposing carbonate and the solid appears to lose mass. Account for the mass change using the general pattern of the breakdown.
items.modelAnswer: The metal carbonate gives a metal oxide and carbon dioxide; the carbon dioxide escapes as a gas, so its mass leaves the tube and the solid that remains appears lighter.

items.stem: Describe the colour change seen when copper(II) carbonate is heated in a test tube.
items.modelAnswer: The green solid darkens little by little as black copper(II) oxide forms.

items.stem: Write the symbol equation for the thermal decomposition of copper(II) carbonate, including the state symbols.
items.modelAnswer: CuCO3 (s) gives CuO (s) + CO2 (g).

items.stem: Explain why limewater turning milky identifies the gas given off in this experiment.
items.modelAnswer: The gas given off is carbon dioxide, and carbon dioxide turns limewater milky, so the milkiness is the positive test that confirms CO2 is the product of the decomposition.

items.stem: 12.40 g of copper(II) carbonate is heated to constant mass and 7.95 g of black solid remains. State the mass that left as gas and name the gas, using the equation of this lesson.
items.modelAnswer: 12.40 - 7.95 = 4.45 g left as carbon dioxide: CuCO3 gives CuO plus CO2, and the escaping CO2 carries the missing mass out of the tube as a gas.

items.stem: What is combustion, and what type of product does every combustion reaction form?
items.modelAnswer: Combustion is the scientific word for burning: oxygen reacts with an element or compound to produce oxides.

items.stem: Name the three combustions of record for this course.
items.modelAnswer: Magnesium, hydrogen and sulfur each burning in oxygen.

items.stem: Explain why every combustion reaction can carry both the labels exothermic and oxidation.
items.modelAnswer: Combustion reactions give out heat, which makes them exothermic, and the burning substance gains oxygen, which makes them oxidation reactions at the same time.

items.stem: A gas heater burns fuel in a room and warms the air. Classify the burning with the two labels of this lesson and state what role the oxygen plays.
items.modelAnswer: Burning the fuel is combustion: it is exothermic because it gives out heat that warms the room, and it is oxidation because the fuel gains oxygen from the air and forms oxides.

items.stem: State the observation and the product when magnesium burns in oxygen.
items.modelAnswer: Magnesium burns with an intense white flame and white magnesium oxide powder is produced.

items.stem: Describe the flame and the product when sulfur burns in oxygen, and give the symbol equation.
items.modelAnswer: Sulfur burns with a blue flame and produces the colourless, poisonous gas sulfur dioxide: S (s) + O2 (g) gives SO2 (g).

items.stem: A student writes the hydrogen equation as H2 + O2 gives H2O. Explain the correction needed and why the corrected form matters.
items.modelAnswer: The equation needs balancing: 2H2 (g) + O2 (g) gives 2H2O (g), because four hydrogen atoms enter on the left and only two would leave on the right; a balanced equation conserves every kind of atom.

items.stem: Three gas jars hold burning magnesium, hydrogen and sulfur. Match each burning substance to its flame colour and name the oxide or product formed in each case.
items.modelAnswer: Magnesium gives an intense white flame and forms magnesium oxide (MgO); hydrogen burns to form water; sulfur gives a blue flame and forms the poisonous gas sulfur dioxide (SO2).

items.stem: State the electron loss and the ion formed when a Group 1 metal takes part in a reaction.
items.modelAnswer: It needs to lose only the single electron in its outer shell, forming a 1+ ion with a full outer shell.

items.stem: Why is the ion formed by a reacting Group 1 metal atom stable?
items.modelAnswer: The filled shell underneath becomes the outermost shell, so the ion gains a noble gas configuration.

items.stem: Account for the shared reaction pattern of the alkali metals using the one-outer-electron structure.
items.modelAnswer: They all share the one-outer-electron pattern: each atom needs to lose only its single outer electron to reach a noble gas configuration, so every alkali metal reacts in the same way.

items.stem: An unseen metal X sits directly below potassium in Group 1. Predict how many electrons one atom of X loses and whether X reacts more or less vigorously than potassium, giving the trend law you used.
items.modelAnswer: One electron: like every Group 1 atom, X loses its single outer electron to form a 1+ ion. X reacts more vigorously than potassium, because reactivity increases down the group.

items.stem: State the shell-count step made at each element on descending from lithium through sodium to potassium.
items.modelAnswer: The number of occupied shells rises by one at each element going down the group.

items.stem: What happens to the amount of energy needed to remove the outer electron on descending Group 1?
items.modelAnswer: Less energy is needed to overcome the weaker attraction, so the outer electron is lost more easily down the group.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of distance and attraction, why potassium's outer electron is lost more easily than sodium's.
items.modelAnswer: The extra shell places potassium's outermost electron further away from the nucleus; the greater distance weakens the pull between the nucleus and that electron, so less energy is needed to remove it and it is lost more easily.

items.stem: Rubidium sits between potassium and caesium in Group 1. Predict whether rubidium's outer electron is lost more or less easily than potassium's, and state the reactivity consequence, using the shell-distance chain.
items.modelAnswer: Rubidium has one more occupied shell than potassium, so its outer electron sits further from the nucleus, the attraction is weaker and the electron is lost more easily; rubidium is therefore more reactive than potassium.

items.stem: Describe how the burette is set up for this oxygen-measuring practical.
items.modelAnswer: Iron filings or a piece of iron wool are placed in the bottom of the closed burette, which is then inverted into a trough of water and clamped vertically.

items.stem: How long is the apparatus left standing, and which readings are taken?
items.modelAnswer: The starting water level is recorded and the burette is read again after 3-4 days.

items.stem: Explain why a little water is used to moisten the inside of the burette before the iron is added.
items.modelAnswer: The iron needs water as well as oxygen to react and rust, so moistening the inside supplies that water and lets the iron consume the oxygen trapped in the burette, which is the change the water level records.

items.stem: Give two design features of this practical that make the trapped air a fixed, fully measured sample, and say why each one matters.
items.modelAnswer: The closed burette inverted into the trough of water seals the air sample inside so no gas can enter or leave, and the dead volume from the last graduation to the tap is measured by draining 50.0 mL of water, so the whole volume of trapped air is known before the wait begins.

items.stem: Show how the initial volume of air, 51.2 mL, is built up in this write-up.
items.modelAnswer: Initial volume of air = (50.0 + 3.8) - 2.6 = 51.2 mL.

items.stem: State what the 10.1 mL obtained by subtracting the final air volume from the initial air volume tells you.
items.modelAnswer: It is the volume of oxygen used up by the iron from the original sample of air.

items.stem: Explain why the conclusion quotes approximately 20 percent rather than an exact figure.
items.modelAnswer: The calculation gives 19.7 percent, which is close to the accepted value of about 20 percent; real readings carry small uncertainties, so the write-up states the approximate figure the evidence supports.

items.stem: A second run with the same initial volume of 51.2 mL ends at 53.9 - 13.0 = 40.9 mL of air. Calculate the oxygen volume and the percentage of oxygen for this run, and state whether it still supports the conclusion.
items.modelAnswer: Oxygen used = 51.2 - 40.9 = 10.3 mL; percentage = 10.3 / 51.2 x 100 = 20.1 percent, so yes, the repeat still agrees with oxygen making up about 20 percent of air.

items.stem: In the heating of zinc with copper(II) oxide, state the equation and identify the reducing agent.
items.modelAnswer: Zn + CuO gives ZnO + Cu on heating; the zinc is the reducing agent because it takes the oxygen for itself.

items.stem: State the displacement rule for metals in one sentence.
items.modelAnswer: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compounds.

items.stem: A crucible holds sodium oxide powder mixed with magnesium powder and is heated strongly. Account for the complete absence of change, using the displacement rule.
items.modelAnswer: Sodium already outranks magnesium in the reactivity series, so magnesium cannot displace sodium from its oxide; only a more reactive metal can take oxygen away from a less reactive one's compound.

items.stem: Magnesium powder is heated with zinc oxide. Predict whether a reaction happens, write the equation, and name the reducing agent.
items.modelAnswer: Magnesium is more reactive than zinc, so it does react: Mg + ZnO gives MgO + Zn, with magnesium acting as the reducing agent by taking the oxygen.

items.stem: Give the word and symbol equations for what happens when magnesium sits in copper(II) sulfate solution.
items.modelAnswer: Magnesium + copper(II) sulfate gives magnesium sulfate + copper: Mg + CuSO4 gives MgSO4 + Cu.

items.stem: State the two observations that show magnesium has displaced copper from copper(II) sulfate solution.
items.modelAnswer: The blue colour of the solution fades as colourless magnesium sulfate forms, and brown copper appears, coating the magnesium surface and falling to the bottom as solid metal.

items.stem: A strip of zinc is left standing in sodium chloride solution overnight. Account for the complete lack of change.
items.modelAnswer: Sodium is more reactive than zinc, so zinc cannot displace sodium from its salt; no more reactive metal is present anywhere in the tube, so no reaction can occur.

items.stem: A metal strip M placed in silver nitrate solution becomes coated with silver while M itself fades into solution. State what this observation proves about M's place in the reactivity series and justify the deduction.
items.modelAnswer: M must be more reactive than silver: only a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its salt, so M goes into solution as its salt forms while silver leaves the solution and coats the strip.

items.stem: What ion do halogen atoms form when they react, and what is its charge called?
items.modelAnswer: A halogen atom gains one electron during reactions to form a -1 ion called a halide ion.

items.stem: Which halogen is the most reactive of the group, and what atomic feature makes it so?
items.modelAnswer: Fluorine is the most reactive halogen in the group because it has the smallest atom.

items.stem: Explain why the reactivity of the Group 7 non-metals falls on descending the group.
items.modelAnswer: The number of electron shells increases by one with each element down the group, so the outer shell lies further from the nucleus; the growing distance weakens the attraction for the electron being gained, making it harder to gain and lowering the reactivity.

items.stem: Astatine sits below iodine in Group 7. Predict whether astatine reacts more or less readily than iodine, and state how many electrons one astatine atom gains when it reacts.
items.modelAnswer: Astatine reacts less readily than iodine, because reactivity decreases down the group; each astatine atom gains one electron to form a -1 halide ion.

items.stem: State the number of outer-shell electrons shared by every Group 7 atom.
items.modelAnswer: All Group 7 atoms have seven electrons in their outermost shell.

items.stem: Going from chlorine to bromine to iodine, what is added to the atom at each step?
items.modelAnswer: One filled shell is added at each element, so the number of shells rises by one on descending the group.

items.stem: Explain why gaining an electron becomes harder for the halogens as the group is descended.
items.modelAnswer: The added shells carry the outermost shell further from the nucleus, so the attraction between the nucleus and the incoming electron grows weaker with distance, and gaining that electron becomes harder, so reactivity falls.

items.stem: Chlorine's outer shell occupies period 3 while bromine's occupies period 4. Using this lesson's distance law, predict which atom attracts an incoming electron more strongly and name the more reactive halogen of the pair.
items.modelAnswer: Chlorine attracts the incoming electron more strongly: its outer shell is one shell closer to the nucleus, so the attraction is greater and the electron is easier to gain, making chlorine the more reactive halogen.
